# Survey sample 

## 1. Survey sampling method 

Surveys were collected using a mix of convenience and random sampling, with the approach varying across the three time periods.  

* 2010: In the 2010 survey period, data were collected by convenience sample only, shared by 23 organizations, including non-profits and foundations, organic certifiers, and departments of agriculture. Surveys were distributed **[JARED please let me know, mail/email process]**. We received a total of 1,029 responses, 545 of which included complete enough data for our analysis. 

* 2015: In the 2015 survey period, data were collected by both random and convenience sampling. For the random sample, 800 certified organic producers were randomly selected from the approximately 12,000 organic producers that use seed recorded in the NOP database. To encourage responsiveness, three follow-up emails were sent following an initial email, paper copies were mailed on request, and individual phone calls were made to follow-up. From these 800, 197 (25%) responded and 127 (16%) were complete enough to use in our analyses. For the convenience sample, surveys were shared by 41 organizations, again including non-profits and foundations, organic certifiers, and departments of agriculture. Surveys were distributed **[JARED please let me know, mail/email process]**. We received a total of 1,148 responses from the convenience sample, 672 of which included complete enough data for our analysis. In total we had 799 usable responses.

* 2020: In the 2020 survey period, again data were collected by both random and convenience sampling. For the random sample, 2,000 certified organic producers were randomly selected from the the NOP database. To encourage responsiveness, the survey was offered as both an online version and a paper questionnaire, and respondents had the option of completing either. After an initial postcard invitation, non-respondents received follow-up contacts by mail, email, and phone. Survey distribution was managed by Washington State University’s Social and Economic Sciences Research Center. From these 2,000 surveys, 448 (22%) responded (206 web surveys and 242 paper surveys) and 193 (10%) were complete enough to use in our analyses. For the convenience sample, surveys were distributed to all remaining certified organic operations over email. For the convenience sample, surveys were shared by OFRF and OSA, social and traditional media, and through organic certifiers and organic farming membership organizations **UPDATE**. We received a total of 611 responses from the convenience sample, 215 of which included complete enough data for our analysis. In total we had 408 usable responses.

The breakdown between random and convenience sampling used in our analysis is summarized in Table 1 and Table 2. We also consider the effect of sampling method, as well as survey distributor, through models in Table 4.

## 2. Checking for biases induced by data collection methods  

In order to test how our data collection methods may bias the sample, we consider the effect of the sampling approach and survey distributor. 

Regarding concerns of sampling approach, we model the effect of sampling method with our 2015 and 2020 survey data (the only survey periods where we had both sampling approaches), including a term for responses that were gathered by random sampling compared to convenience sampling (Table 4, Model 1). We see a small and insignificant effect for sampling method, and negligible changes in the results between the models run with and without the sampling consideration (Table 4, Model 2). 

Regarding concerns of survey distributor (i.e. that the distribution by Organic Seed Alliance (OSA) elicited responses from a select type of organic farmer), we model the effect of sampling method with our 2010 and 2015 survey data (the only survey periods that identified specific distributors), including a term for responses that were gathered by OSA compared to all others (Table 4, Model 3). We see a small and insignificant effect for distributor, and negligible changes in the results between the models run with and without the sampling consideration (Table 4, Model 4). 


## 3. Sample representativeness 

While the mix of sampling methods creates a challenge for determining the sample's representativeness of the population, we aim to demonstrate that our sample is representative by comparing the geographic distribution and approximate average farm size of our sample to USDA Agricultural Census data. We use USDA Census data from 2011, 2016, and 2021 to align with our 2010, 2015, and 2020 survey periods. 

Across the three survey periods, the number of respondents represented approximately 6.3%, 5.9%, and 2.5% of the total number of organic farmers identified in the USDA Census in the related years, though these timelines are not exactly set to match. 

In Table 3 we compare the number of operations in our sample (n) to the population (N) by year and region. For each census period we calculated the standard deviation of the percentage of operations represented, which we used to identify regions that are over or under-represented (mean of % operations represented +/- sd of % operations represented). Over-represented year-region combinations are signaled by green text, while under-represented year-region combinations are signaled by red text. Only in 2011 do we see variation in representation across regions, with the North Central and Western regions over-represented and the Northeast under-represented. 

We also calculate the mean acreage in our sample, as well as the mean acreage according to the USDA census (N operations/total acreage) for a given year-region combination. Using the mean here provides limited information, given that farm sizes vary considerably in ways that are not captured in aggregate data available in the USDA census. Though crude, these averages suggest relative similarity in average farm size.

```{r, echo = F, message = F, warning = F}
tablea3 <- read.csv('tables/append_rept1.csv') 
tablea3 <- tablea3 %>% 
  group_by(survey_year) %>%   
  summarize(mean_rep = round(100*(sum(sample_n_operations)/sum(usda_census_n_operations)), 2)) %>% 
  right_join(tablea3) %>% 
  mutate(meansd_ul = mean_rep + sd(representativeness_ops),
         meansd_ll = mean_rep - sd(representativeness_ops))
## Should I be using mean_rep or mean(tablea3$representativeness_ops)??
mean_reps <- unique(tablea3$mean_rep)
tablea3$representativeness_ops = cell_spec(tablea3$representativeness_ops, 
                                         color = ifelse(tablea3$representativeness_ops > tablea3$meansd_ul, "green", 
                                                 ifelse(tablea3$representativeness_ops < tablea3$meansd_ll, "red", "black")))
tablea3 <- select(tablea3, -c(mean_rep, meansd_ul, meansd_ll))
colnames(tablea3) <- c("Year", "Region", "Operations in sample (n)",
                        #"Proportion of\ntotal n", 
                       "Operations in USDA census (N)",
                        #"Proportion of\ntotal N", 
                       #"Operation\nrepresentation",
                       "Percent of operations represented (n/N)",
                        "Mean acreage in sample", "Mean acreage in USDA Census",
                        "Mean acreage difference")

kbl(tablea3, booktabs = T, escape = F, align = c(rep('l', 2), rep('c', 6)),
    caption = 'Sample representativeness compared to USDA Censuses (2011, 2016, 2021)') %>% 
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position")) %>% 
  #kableExtra::landscape() %>% 
  column_spec(1:8, 
              width = c('1cm','2.2cm','1.8cm','2cm', '2.8cm', 
                        '2cm', '2.2cm', '2cm'))
```


```{r, echo = F, eval = F, message = F, warning = F}

  right_join(tablea3) %>% 
  mutate(meansd_ul = mean_rep + sd(representativeness_ops),
         meansd_ll = mean_rep - sd(representativeness_ops))
## Should I be using mean_rep or mean(tablea3$representativeness_ops)??
tablea3$mean_rep
tablea3$representativeness_ops = cell_spec(tablea3$representativeness_ops, 
                                         color = ifelse(tablea3$representativeness_ops > tablea3$meansd_ul, "green", 
                                                 ifelse(tablea3$representativeness_ops < tablea3$meansd_ll, "red", "black")))
tablea3 <- select(tablea3, -c(mean_rep, meansd_ul, meansd_ll))
colnames(tablea3) <- c("Year", "Crop category",  "Region", 
                       "Operations in\nsample (n)",
                        #"Proportion of\ntotal n",

                        #"Proportion of\ntotal N",

                       "Operation representativeness",
                        "Mean acreage\nin sample", "Mean acreage\nUSDA Census",

kbl(tablea3, booktabs = T, escape = F, align = c(rep('l', 3), rep('c', 6)),
    caption = 'Sample representativeness compared to USDA Censuses (2011, 2016, 2021)') %>% 
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position")) %>% 
  #kableExtra::landscape() %>% 
  column_spec(3:9, width = '2.2cm') %>% 
  column_spec(1:8, extra_css = "vertical-align:middle;")
```


To try to better compare the representativeness of farm size, we look at the only available nationally reported data on organic farm size distribution that we could find: USDA Census organic tabulations, reporting for the [2012](https://agcensus.library.cornell.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012-organictab-1.pdf) and [2017](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/AgCensus/2017/Online_Resources/Organics_Tabulation/organictab.pdf) censuses. 

We compare these USDA Census data against our survey sample, presented in Figure 1. These comparisons show a consistent over-representation of the smallest farms (1-9 acres) by 12-18% and under-representation of the largest farms.  Still, we have faith that our sample captures the overall distribution of organic farm size. Additionally, an important consideration is that we calculate farm size as reported acreage planted to three major crop categories. This approach likely underestimates acreage generally compared to USDA approach, which reports all certified land.  

```{r fig1, echo = F, out.width = '100%', fig.pos='H', fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = 'Sample farm size distribution compared to USDA Organic Census data'}
knitr::include_graphics('~/Documents/Davis/R-Projects/organicseed_adoption/figures/append_repf1_usda.png', rel_path = getOption("knitr.graphics.rel_path", FALSE))
```

## 6. Mediation analyses  

To check for mediated effects of values and barriers on operational attributes, we run three mediation analyses. A mediating variable is one that transmits the effect one variable to another

We first addresses the potential mediation effect of larger farms on valuing organic seed. In other words, are those who value organic seed more likely to have smaller farms, and if so, how might that affect the model results? We depict a simplified representation of this mediating effect in Figure 2. 

```{r med1 diagram, results = "asis", echo = F, out.width = '75%', fig.pos='H', fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = 'Mediation diagram: Organic seed value and farm size'}
DiagrammeR::grViz("
digraph {
  graph []
  node [shape = plaintext]
    X [label ='Values organic seed', shape = box, color = black]
    Y [label ='Proportion acreage planted to organic seed', shape = box, color = black]
    M [label ='Farm size', shape = box]
  edge [minlen = 2]
    X->M  
    M->Y 
    X->Y [color = black]
  { rank = same; X; Y; M }
}
")
```


We run a mediation analysis by comparing results of our full regression model (e.g. results in Table 5) with results of a model that regresses the same variables on the potential mediator: farm size. Results are presented in Table 6, where the Average Causal Mediation Effect (ACME) is significant. This result suggests the effect of organic seed values on organic seed use (Total Effect) is mediated by farm size. 
```{r mediation1, echo = F}
table <- read.csv('tables/append_mediation1.csv')  
colnames(table) <- c("Effects", "Estimate", "p-value")
kbl(table, align = 'c', booktabs = T, 
    caption = 'Mediation analysis of farm size on quantity barrier') %>% kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position"))
  #column_spec(2:4, width = '4cm')
```

Next we addresses the potential mediation effect of experiencing organic seed quantity barriers on larger farms. In other words, might larger farms be more likely to experience the barrier of limited organic seed quantity, and if so, how might that affect the model results? We depict a simplified representation of this mediating effect in Figure 2. 
```{r med2 diagram, results = "asis", echo = F, out.width = '75%', fig.pos='H', fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = 'Mediation diagram: Farm size and organic seed quantity'}
DiagrammeR::grViz("
digraph {
  graph []
  node [shape = plaintext]
    X [label ='Farm size', shape = box, color = black]
    Y [label ='Proportion acreage planted to organic seed', shape = box, color = black]
    M [label ='Barrier: Insufficient quantity', shape = box]
  edge [minlen = 2]
    X->M  
    M->Y 
    X->Y [color = black]
  { rank = same; X; Y; M }
}
")
```

We run a mediation analysis by comparing results of our full regression model (e.g. results in Table 5) with results of a model that regresses the same variables on the potential mediator: the quantity barrier. Results are presented in Table 6, where the Average Causal Mediation Effect (ACME) is small (-0.001) and not significant. The value suggests how much the effect of farm size on organic seed use (Total Effect) is mediated by this barrier. In this case, the mediated effect is small and the total and Average Direct Effects (ADE) are larger and significant. In short, the quantity barrier is not influencing the effect of farm size. 
```{r mediation2, echo = F}
table <- read.csv('tables/append_mediation2.csv')  
colnames(table) <- c("Effects", "Estimate", "p-value")
kbl(table, align = 'c', booktabs = T, 
    caption = 'Mediation analysis of farm size on quantity barrier') %>% kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position"))
  #column_spec(2:4, width = '4cm')
```

Next we addresses the potential mediation effect of experiencing organic seed availability barriers on more diverse farms. In other words, are farms that use a wider variety of seeds more likely to experience the barrier of limited organic seed availability, and if so, how might that affect the model results? We depict a simplified representation of this mediating effect in Figure 3. 
```{r med3 diagram,echo = F, out.width = '75%', fig.pos='H', fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = 'Mediation diagram: Crop diversity and organic seed availability'}
DiagrammeR::grViz("
digraph {
  graph []
  node [shape = plaintext]
    X [label ='Crop diversity', shape = box, color = black]
    Y [label ='Proportion acreage planted to organic seed', shape = box, color = black]
    M [label ='Barrier: Availability', shape = box]
  edge [minlen = 2]
    X->M  
    M->Y 
    X->Y [color = black]
  { rank = same; X; Y; M }
}
")
```

Again, we run a mediation analysis by comparing results of our full regression model with results of a model that regresses the same variables on the potential mediator: the availability barrier. Results are presented in Table 7, where again the ACME is small (-0.002) and not significant. In short, the availability barrier is not influencing the effect of crop diversity. 

```{r mediation3, echo = F}
table <- read.csv('tables/append_mediation3.csv')  
colnames(table) <- c("Effects", "Estimate", "p-value")
kbl(table, align = 'c', booktabs = T, 
    caption = 'Mediation analysis of crop diversity on availability barrier') %>% kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position"))
  #column_spec(2:4, width = '4cm')
```

## 9. Certifiers' role

An additional consideration in our analysis is the effect of certifier. We expect certifiers to enforce the regulation differently **(cite)**, but  we do not have data that allows us to specifically identify each producers' certifier in our data for use in our main analysis. However, we do have some suggestion of growers' certifier based on our data collection process in certain survey periods. When data are available, we assume that respondents who completed the survey distributed by a certain certifier are certified by them. In Table 9, Model 1 we model the effect of five distinct certifiers and one 'other' category, compared against compared to a baseline of the most popular certifier in our limited dataset. We see a small and insignificant effect for different certifiers compared to a baseline certifier group, and negligible changes in the results between the models run with and without the sampling consideration (Table 9, Model 2). 

```{r cert model, echo = F, results = "asis"}
m_list <- readRDS('tables/append_certifier_model.RDS')
stargazer::stargazer(m_list,  type = "latex", 
           dep.var.labels = "\\shortstack{Proportion of production acreage\\\\planted with organic seed}", 
           covariate.labels = c(core_vars2[-9],"Certifier Other",
                                "Certifier 24", "Certifier 2", "Certifier 27",
                                "Certifier 42", "Certifier 7", "Constant"), 
           model.numbers = T, nobs = TRUE, dep.var.caption = "", 
           no.space = TRUE, header = FALSE, intercept.bottom = T,
           title = "Model checks for certifier effects", 
           table.placement = "H", keep.stat = c("n", "ll", 'rsq'),
           label=knitr::opts_current$get("label"))
```
